The first is concentration: a driveway is a smooth, compacted, nearly impermeable surface, so rain that lands on it does not soak in — it sheets across and gathers. Wherever the driveway's crown or slope lets the sheet gather into a rivulet — at a low corner, where a slope break occurs, where the drive meets a steeper pitch — the flow stops being a harmless sheet and becomes a small stream with real erosive power. The second suspect is the wheel rut: traffic compacts two tracks into the gravel, and those tracks become pre-formed channels that intercept the sheet flow and focus it. A focused stream on loose gravel does what any stream does to loose sediment — it entrains the particles it can move, which is to say your driveway, and delivers them to the lowest exit, the road.

The spots are the same because the geometry is the same: the water is not choosing them capriciously, it is reporting them. That is also the logic of the standard fixes. A proper crown — the driveway's center a few centimetres higher than its edges — sheds water off the sides before it can gather; water bars or cross-drains intercept flow on slopes before it gains volume; and ditches give the intercepted water somewhere legal to go. Particle size plays its part too: angular, mixed-size gravel (with fines that lock the surface) resists entrainment far better than rounded, uniform pea gravel, which rolls like ball bearings.

Whether your two spots need regrading, a cross-drain, or just better gravel is a site judgment — but diagnose them as plumbing, not as gravel failure. The gravel is fine. It is being mined by a stream your driveway accidentally built.
My grandfather dug a farm pond 40 years ago and it was deep enough to swim in. Now it's half the depth and filling with cattails. Nobody's dumping anything in it. Where is the depth going?

The pond is being filled by its own watershed, one storm at a time — a pond is a sediment trap, and sediment traps fill. Every stream and slope draining into the pond carries a load: soil eroded from the banks and fields upstream, delivered in pulses during storms. In the flowing stream that load stays suspended or bounces along the bed, but the moment the water enters the pond it slows to near stillness, and still water cannot carry sediment. The load settles out on the pond floor. The pond, in other words, is doing to its watershed exactly what a delta does to a river — it is where the current dies, so it is where the sediment lands, and the floor rises a little with every muddy inflow. Decades of storms is a lot of little.

The cattails are the second phase, and they accelerate the first. As the margins shallow, emergent plants colonize them; their stems slow the water further and trap more sediment, and their own dead growth adds organic muck to the fill. The pond shallows, warms, grows richer in nutrients and plants, and fills faster — ecologists call the whole progression pond succession, and its endpoint, left alone, is a marsh and then a wet meadow where the pond used to be. Your grandfather did not dig a permanent feature; he dug a temporary one with a lifespan set by the erosion rate of everything uphill of it.

Reversing it means either dredging — removing the accumulated sediment mechanically, which resets the clock but not the rate — or reducing the delivery: stabilizing eroding banks and keeping a vegetated buffer around the pond to filter inflows. Either way, the governing fact is the budget: a pond's depth is the difference between what its watershed delivers and what anyone removes. Your pond has been running a surplus for forty years.

Our pond covers about 2,000 square metres and the creek feeding it drops roughly 40 cubic metres of sediment into it a year. The pond averages about 2 metres deep. At this rate, how fast is it filling, and how long until it's basically full?
The fill rate per year is the sediment volume spread over the pond's area. Working in centimetres of depth per year:
2 centimetres of depth lost per year. Your 2-metre average depth is 200 centimetres, so the time to fill at that rate is:

About 100 years to fill completely — which means the pond loses a fifth of its depth every 20 years, well within the horizon of someone maintaining it across a lifetime. That is the arithmetic behind the familiar sight of a 'grandfather's pond' that grandchildren find half gone: nobody neglected it in any dramatic way; 2 centimetres a year simply never sent a bill.

Now the honest adjustments, in both directions. The fill will not stay linear: as the pond shallows, vegetation colonizes the margins, traps sediment more efficiently, and adds its own organic debris, so the later decades usually fill faster than the early ones. Working the other way, fresh sediment compacts under its own weight — a loose 40 cubic metres delivered becomes somewhat less once consolidated — and big floods can occasionally scour as well as deposit. And the 40 cubic metres itself is the softest number here: it is set by erosion in the whole watershed, so a single badly eroding bank upstream can double it.

But as a planning figure it does its job: at centimetres per year, dredging is a once-in-a-generation project, and cutting the sediment delivery — stabilizing the creek banks, buffering the shore — is worth more than any single dredging, because it changes the rate rather than the balance.
My house is on a hill — I can see the whole neighborhood below me — yet my basement floods in wet springs. How can the high house be the wet one?

Because 'on a hill' describes the surface, and basements flood from the subsurface, which has its own topography. Three mechanisms commonly soak the hilltop house. The first is a perched water table: if a layer of clay or dense material lies a few metres down, water percolating from the surface cannot pass it, so it accumulates on top of the layer, forming a saturated zone perched above the true water table. Your basement, dug down into the hill, may extend right into that perched zone — you have built a dry-looking pit into a hidden pond, and in wet springs the perched water rises against your walls and finds the cracks.

The second is surface drainage lying to you at small scale: the hill is high, but the grading immediately around the house — settled backfill along the foundation, a patio or drive sloping inward, downspouts discharging at the wall — can collect the roof and lot's runoff and deliver it precisely to the foundation, hill or no hill. The third is the hillside itself: groundwater moving through the hill along a permeable layer can daylight into your excavation the way a spring daylights on a slope; a basement dug into a hillside is, hydrologically, a hole poked into the hill's plumbing, and hillside springs choose such holes.

Which of the three is yours is a diagnosis, not a guess: water arriving after rain at one wall suggests drainage or perched water; a steady seep in a wet season suggests the hillside flow. A local waterproofing contractor or geotechnical engineer can tell them apart with a site visit and, sometimes, a test pit. But release the intuition that elevation is protection. Elevation protects you from other people's water. It does nothing about your own hill's.
A storm dropped 20 mm of rain on my house, which has a roof footprint of about 150 square metres. My downspout tore a trench in the flower bed below it. How much water actually came off that roof?
More than intuition suggests. A useful identity: 1 millimetre of rain on 1 square metre is exactly 1 litre. So your roof harvested:
3,000 litres. In cubic metres:

3 cubic metres — three tonnes of water, collected from a modest storm by a modest roof, and concentrated by your gutter system into a few downspouts. That concentration is the whole story of the trench: spread over the roof, 20 mm is a gentle wetting; gathered to one outlet and dropped in a jet, it is a fire hose running for the duration of the storm, and loose flower-bed soil has no defense against it. Garden soil erodes under a downspout not because the rain was extreme but because the roof is a rain-collecting machine that converts area into flow at a point.

The fixes all follow from the arithmetic: give the jet somewhere armored to land (a splash block, a bed of stone), pipe it away to a place that can accept three tonnes spread out (a lawn, a rain garden, a dry well), or spread it yourself with a rain chain or a perforated extension. Note also what the number implies for rain barrels: a single barrel of a couple of hundred litres captures only a small first slice of a storm like this — barrels are for watering cans, not storm management. Roofs are watersheds in miniature, and they obey watershed rules.
One corner of my backyard is always soggy, even in dry weeks when the rest of the lawn is crisp. It's not near any pipe. What could make one patch of ground stay wet?

Several underground suspects can keep one patch wet, and they are distinguishable by their habits. The most common is a clay lens: a body of fine-grained soil buried in otherwise freer-draining ground. Water percolating down hits the lens, cannot pass at any speed, and accumulates above it as a little perched reservoir that keeps the surface soil damp long after the rest of the yard has dried. A close relative is compaction — if that corner was a construction staging area, a parking spot, or a path, its soil structure may be crushed enough to behave like the clay lens even without clay.

The second suspect is geometry: your corner may be the subtle low of the lot, the place the whole yard's subsurface drainage converges — the swale's end. Surface dryness misleads here; water can be moving toward that corner underground along the top of a denser layer even when no surface flow is visible. The third is a genuine seep: on any lot with the slightest slope, groundwater moving through a permeable layer can be forced upward or outward where the layer thins or meets a barrier, producing a permanently damp patch that is, in effect, a small, shy spring. That one betrays itself by staying wettest in the wet season and by the water being cool.

A French drain — a gravel-filled trench with a perforated pipe — is the usual remedy for the first two, because it gives the perched or converging water an easy path to somewhere legal. But the right fix depends on which suspect you have, and a soggy patch that is actually a seep or, worse, a leaking service line deserves identification before excavation. The cheap diagnostic is a dry-week one: dig a small hole in the patch. If it slowly fills with water from the bottom, you are looking at groundwater or a perched table, not surface drainage — and that distinction decides everything downstream.
Regulations say a septic system has to be a certain distance from a well — like 30 metres. Is that number based on something real, or is it just bureaucratic round numbers?

It is based on something real, though the something is a proxy. The actual safety variable is time: the time groundwater takes to travel from the drain field to the well. Pathogens — bacteria, viruses — die off or are filtered and adsorbed as water moves through soil, so if the journey takes long enough, the water arriving at the well has been cleansed by the trip. Distance is regulated because distance is measurable with a tape, while travel time depends on the local seepage velocity, which nobody can read off the surface. The setback is a distance chosen so that, in typical soils, the implied travel time exceeds the survival time of the pathogens of concern, with margin to spare.

But notice what the round number hides, because the mechanism reveals two ways the rule can mislead. First, direction matters more than distance: a septic field 30 metres from a well but directly upgradient of it, with groundwater flowing from field to well, is far more dangerous than one 20 metres away downgradient, where the flow carries effluent away from the well forever. Setback circles are blind to flow direction; aquifers are not. Second, velocity varies by orders of magnitude with the material: 30 metres through clayey silt might be a journey of years, while 30 metres through coarse gravel or fractured rock — or worse, through karst limestone with its open conduits — might take days, less than pathogen survival times. That is why codes quietly adjust: many jurisdictions demand larger setbacks in coarse or fractured ground, and why a site evaluation looks at soil and slope, not just the tape measure.

So the number is a bureaucratic round figure built on a real mechanism — a travel-time rule wearing a distance costume, adequate in the average ground it was written for, and worth a second look wherever the ground is faster, or the flow is aimed the wrong way.

The culvert under my driveway keeps overwhelming in big storms. Its little catchment is about 8,000 square metres. In a storm that drops 30 mm of rain, if about 60% runs off, how much water is the culvert being asked to pass, and how fast?
Build the volume first. The catchment is 8,000 square metres and the storm delivers 30 millimetres, which is 0.03 metres:
240 cubic metres of rain on the catchment. At 60% runoff:
144 cubic metres actually heading for your culvert. Now the rate: if that runoff arrives over roughly an hour — a reasonable sketch for a small catchment in a heavy storm — the average flow is:

0.04 cubic metres per second — 40 litres every second, sustained for an hour, through a pipe that also has to swallow the peak, which on a small catchment can run well above the hourly average because the whole area contributes at once. That is the intuition your overwhelmed culvert is teaching: small areas and modest storms still produce bathtub-per-second flows, because area multiplies so efficiently.

Treat this strictly as intuition, not a design. Real culvert sizing uses local rainfall-intensity records for a chosen design storm, a runoff coefficient matched to the actual surfaces, and the time it takes the farthest water to reach the pipe — and undersizing has consequences beyond a wet driveway, including washing out the drive itself and flooding upstream neighbors. A local civil engineer or your county road department sizes driveway culverts routinely and cheaply relative to the damage. What the arithmetic gives you is respect for the problem: 144 cubic metres is not a drainage detail, it is a small river with an appointment at your driveway.
